name: Methodist Episcopal Church
summary: The principal early American Methodist denomination, organized after independence to provide its own ministry and sacramental life.
formation_narrative: The American Revolution disrupted Anglican structures that had served Methodist societies. Wesley commissioned Thomas Coke, and the Christmas Conference in Baltimore organized the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1784 with Francis Asbury as a central leader. An itinerant ministry helped it expand widely. Slavery, authority, and representation later generated divisions; northern and southern branches participated in the 1939 Methodist reunion.
core_beliefs: Grace and response: salvation begins with God’s grace, calls for faith, and leads into a transformed life.
Holiness: love of God and neighbor is the aim of Christian growth, not merely formal membership.
Connectional practice: preaching, sacraments, disciplined fellowship, and mission join personal faith to shared church life.

name: Methodist Episcopal Church, South
notes: Formed in 1845 after a split over slavery; merged in 1939.
summary: The southern Methodist body created after the slavery-related division of the Methodist Episcopal Church.
formation_narrative: The 1844 conflict over slavery and episcopal authority led to separate southern organization in 1845. The resulting church preserved much Methodist doctrine while institutionalizing a sectional division tied to slaveholding. It entered the 1939 union with northern Methodists and Methodist Protestants. Explaining this as merely administrative geography would obscure the moral and political conflict behind the separation.
core_beliefs: Wesleyan inheritance: grace, conversion, sanctification, and Methodist preaching remained central.
Episcopal connection: bishops and conferences organized ministry across congregations.
Doctrine and slavery: shared confessional ancestry did not prevent leaders from taking opposing positions on slavery; the separation was not a new doctrine of salvation.

name: Methodist Protestant Church
notes: Separated from the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1828; merged in 1939.
summary: A Methodist body that challenged episcopal concentration of authority and sought greater representative participation.
formation_narrative: Reformers dissatisfied with Methodist governance organized the Associated Methodist Churches in 1828 and adopted the Methodist Protestant name in 1830. Their dispute centered on representation and church government rather than abandonment of Wesleyan faith. Most of the body joined the 1939 Methodist union. Some official summaries compress the process to an 1828 split, so the two milestones should be distinguished.
core_beliefs: Wesleyan teaching: conversion, grace, and growth in holiness remained part of the movement’s inheritance.
Representative government: reformers sought a stronger voice for laypeople and ministers in church decision-making.
Non-episcopal organization: rejecting bishop-centered government did not mean rejecting cooperative conferences or shared discipline.

name: Methodist Church
notes: Formed in 1939 by reunion of MEC, MECS, and MPC; merged into the UMC in 1968.
summary: The American church formed in 1939 by union of three major Methodist bodies and later a parent of the United Methodist Church.
formation_narrative: The Methodist Episcopal Church, Methodist Episcopal Church South, and Methodist Protestant Church united in 1939. Reunion overcame longstanding sectional and governmental divisions but did not erase the history of racial exclusion in American Methodism. The combined body later joined the Evangelical United Brethren in 1968. Its identity therefore combines a new institutional union with older Wesleyan doctrinal continuity.
core_beliefs: Wesleyan continuity: grace, faith, and sanctification remained foundational despite the union of different institutional histories.
Connectional ministry: congregations shared oversight, mission, and educational institutions through conferences.
Unity with unresolved tensions: institutional reunion did not itself settle every question of racial equality or church governance.

name: Evangelical United Brethren Church
notes: Formed in 1946 by merger of Evangelical Church and United Brethren in Christ; merged into the UMC in 1968.
summary: A church formed in 1946 from two revival traditions rooted in German-speaking American Christianity.
formation_narrative: The Evangelical Church and United Brethren in Christ united in 1946 after developing parallel traditions of evangelical preaching and Christian discipleship. Their earlier leaders ministered among German-speaking communities in a religious environment influenced by Pietism and Methodism. In 1968 the EUB joined the Methodist Church to create the United Methodist Church. The earlier founders belong to its ancestry rather than the 1946 organizing generation.
core_beliefs: Evangelical conversion: preaching called people to personal trust in Christ and a changed life.
Holy living: inward faith was expected to produce practical Christian conduct.
Shared confession and ministry: the EUB Confession of Faith later became one of the doctrinal standards inherited by the United Methodist Church.

name: United Methodist Church
notes: Formed in 1968 by merger of the Methodist Church and the Evangelical United Brethren Church.
summary: A worldwide Methodist church created in 1968 from Methodist and Evangelical United Brethren traditions.
formation_narrative: The 1968 union brought together two American connectional churches with overlapping revival and holiness histories. United Methodism links local congregations through conferences and an episcopal system and joins personal discipleship to service and mission. Its contemporary history includes substantial disagreements and departures; the dataset’s lineage is introductory and does not yet represent all recent branches or regions.
core_beliefs: Grace and response: salvation begins with God’s grace, calls for faith, and leads into a transformed life.
Holiness: love of God and neighbor is the aim of Christian growth, not merely formal membership.
Connectional practice: preaching, sacraments, disciplined fellowship, and mission join personal faith to shared church life.
